findings.title: Unauthenticated /rest/memories exposes all user accounts with password hashes, deluxe tokens and TOTP secrets
findings.analysis: GET /rest/memories (no authentication) returns HTTP 200 with all memory records; each record embeds the full user object containing email, role, a 32-hex password hash, deluxeToken and totpSecret. Control comparison: /rest/wallet/balance and /api/Users/ correctly require an Authorization header (401 without auth), so the leak is specific to /rest/memories. Observed fresh on this target instance: 2026-10-04T23:47Z and 2026-10-04T23:55Z; response 200, wrapped {"status":"success","data":[...]} with 2 records, each User object showing password (MD5-derivable 32-hex), role and deluxeToken. Impact: an unauthenticated actor can enumerate registered emails and roles and harvest secret-bearing values (password hashes, premium tokens, TOTP secrets).
findings.false_positive_check: The response is not an error page or a null/empty default: status 200 with a populated data array and real user objects whose fields (password, deluxeToken, totpSecret) are the same shapes seen in authenticated endpoints. Other endpoints (/rest/wallet/balance, /api/Users/) are correctly 401 without auth, so this is a targeted missing authorization guard, not a framework default.

findings.title: Account existence enumerable via /rest/user/security-question?email= (information disclosure / account enumeration)
findings.analysis: GET /rest/user/security-question?email=X returns an HTTP 200 response whose BODY STRUCTURE differs deterministically: an existing email yields {"question":{"id":7,"question":"Name of your favorite pet?","createdAt":...}} while a nonexistent email yields {}. Verified fresh against bjoern@owasp.org (question returned) and nz_999@juice-sh.op (empty {}), both HTTP 200. This converts any leaked email list (e.g., from BHB-002) into a confirmed-registration list with security-question metadata, enabling targeted password-recovery abuse or phishing.
findings.false_positive_check: Both cases are HTTP 200 (not a 4xx/5xx that could indicate a broken route), and the difference is in response body content rather than status code, ruling out an endpoint-missing explanation. The behavior is consistent across repeated probes.

findings.title: Deluxe membership can be obtained without payment by client-specified paymentMode=free (Broken Access Control / financial)
findings.analysis: POST /rest/deluxe-membership accepts a client-controlled paymentMode field. A customer-authenticated request with body {"paymentMode":"free","paymentId":""} returns HTTP 200 with {"status":"success","data":{"confirmation":"Congratulations! You are now a deluxe member!","token":<new JWT>}} — the user's role is promoted to deluxe and a new deluxeToken is issued with NO payment completed. Verified on two fresh customer accounts (researcherY, researcherZ) on 2026-10-04T23:50Z: the first variant {"paymentMode":"free","paymentId":""} grants deluxe (200); the variant {"paymentMode":"free","paymentId":"x"} (non-empty paymentId) is rejected with 400; a creditCard request without a valid paymentId fails with an error. The secure baseline is that paymentMode is server-selected and the payment is required before role promotion.
findings.false_positive_check: The endpoint is not a misconfiguration returning generic success for all payloads: variants with non-empty paymentId or without paymentMode=free are rejected with 400/error. The success response contains a new JWT whose role claim is deluxe, independently confirmable via /rest/user/whoami (role field). The bypass requires no payment and no admin access — a customer account alone.

findings.title: CAPTCHA answer leaked by GET /rest/captcha (information disclosure; bypass not reproducible in this variant)
findings.analysis: GET /rest/captcha returns the server-computed answer alongside the challenge: {"captchaId":N,"captcha":"<math expression>","answer":"<computed result>"} (e.g. captchaId=20, "1-5+3" -> -17). The answer field is the secret needed to pass server-side captcha validation. However, in this activation's mutation the CAPTCHA Bypass via POST /api/Feedbacks/ could not be reproduced: exhaustive request variants (mathematically correct expression alone, expression + echoed answer, minimal payloads, with/without UserId/rating/comment, both field names) all returned 401 "Wrong answer to CAPTCHA. Please try again." The leak is confirmed as an information disclosure; the full bypass impact was tested and is not demonstrated in this variant.
findings.false_positive_check: The answer value matches independent evaluation of the expression (e.g. 1-5+3 = -17, verified with Python eval), so it is a server-computed value, not a template placeholder or client-side guess. The leak is therefore genuine; the negative result on the bypass is a separate, also-reproduced observation.

findings.title: Authenticated non-admin customers can enumerate all user accounts incl. admin roles via GET /api/Users/ (Broken Access Control)
findings.analysis: GET /api/Users/ requires authentication (401 without a token) but does not restrict the returned user list by role. A customer-authenticated request (customer JWT) returns HTTP 200 with the full list of 26 users, including 8 admin-role accounts (admin@juice-sh.op, bkimminich/bjoern.kimminich@gmail.com, support@juice-sh.op, J12934@juice-sh.op, wurstbrot@juice-sh.op, ...), each with email and role. The same endpoint with no auth is 401, and /rest/user/whoami with the customer token returns {"user":{}}. The frontend bundle contains an admin user-management table (userDataSource/paginatorUsers), indicating the user list is an admin function; a customer bypassing to view all admin accounts is inconsistent with a role-restricted design.
findings.false_positive_check: The 401 without auth proves the endpoint is intended to be protected, and the customer JWT is valid for other endpoints (wallet/balance returns 0, order-history returns []). The response contains real admin-role rows, not a generic default. Caveat: this is observed behavior; whether the base design intends admin-only restriction is inferred from the admin-scoped use of the list in the frontend and the endpoint's auth requirement.
